question:
The sentence given below contains some spelling errors. Select the option that has the correct spellings.

Memberrs of the asocciation have succesfully climbed several paeks of the Himalayan range.
option_1: Members of the associattion have succesfully climbed several paeks of the Himalayan range.
option_2: Meembers of the associatiion have successfuly climbed several peaks of the Himalayan range.
option_3: Members of the associasion have succesfully climbed several paiks of the Himalayan range.
option_4: Members of the association have successfully climbed several peaks of the Himalayan range.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Members of the association have successfully climbed several peaks of the Himalayan range.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence contains four misspelt words — "Memberrs", "asocciation", "succesfully" and "paeks". Only Option 4 corrects all four of them at the same time.

◦ Memberrs → Members (MEM + BERS; only one "r").

◦ asocciation → association (AS + SO + CI + A + TION; double "s", single "c").

◦ succesfully → successfully (SUC + CESS + FUL + LY; double "c", double "s", single "l" in "-ful" + "-ly").

◦ paeks → peaks (PEAK = the pointed top of a mountain).

• Correct sentence: Members of the association have successfully climbed several peaks of the Himalayan range.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 still keeps "associattion", "succesfully" and "paeks" wrong.

• Option 2 keeps "Meembers", "associatiion" and "successfuly" wrong.

• Option 3 keeps "associasion", "succesfully" and "paiks" wrong.

NOTE

• Useful meanings: association (संघ/संस्था) = an organised group of people; peak (शिखर) = the top of a mountain; successfully (सफलतापूर्वक) = in a way that achieves the desired result.

• Do not confuse peak (mountain top), peek (a quick look) and pique (to annoy / arouse interest).

question: Choose the sentence that contains an error.
option_1: The Mona Lisa is a famous painting by Leonardo da Vinci.
option_2: She is the only person who can speak five languages fluently.
option_3: He is a doctor who specialises in the treating rare diseases.
option_4: I saw the movie that won the Academy Award for Best Picture.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He is a doctor who specialises in the treating rare diseases.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The article "the" is wrongly placed before the gerund "treating". When a gerund is followed directly by its object ("rare diseases"), it does not take an article.

◦ Incorrect: He is a doctor who specialises in the treating rare diseases.

◦ Correct: He is a doctor who specialises in treating rare diseases. (or — "in the treatment of rare diseases")

• "Specialise in + V-ing" is the fixed structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is correct — "The Mona Lisa" is a specific painting, so "the" is right, and "by Leonardo da Vinci" shows the agent.

• Option 2 is correct — "the only person who" uses the correct relative pronoun for a person, and "fluently" (adverb) correctly modifies "speak".

• Option 4 is correct — "the movie that won" uses a proper defining relative clause.

NOTE

• Rule for gerunds: "the" + gerund + "of" + object ("the treating of rare diseases") OR bare gerund + object ("treating rare diseases"). Mixing the two — "the treating rare diseases" — is always wrong.

• Similar: "in the writing of letters" / "in writing letters" (both fine), but NOT "in the writing letters".

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.

The conferrence / attempts to / trace the processes and / consequences of climate change.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The conferrence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Conferrence" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "conference" — a formal meeting for discussion. (सम्मेलन)

◦ Spelling key: CON + FER + ENCE — only one "r".

◦ Correct: The conference attempts to trace the processes and consequences of climate change.

• Learners often double the "r" by analogy with "referred/preferred", but in "conference" the stress shifts to the first syllable, so the "r" is not doubled.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "attempts to", "trace the processes and" and "consequences of climate change" are all correctly spelt.

• "consequences" (परिणाम) = results or effects; "processes" (प्रक्रियाएँ) = a series of actions or steps.

NOTE

• Same family: confer (to discuss / to award), conferred, conferring — these DO double the "r" — but the noun conference does not.

• Other commonly misspelt "-ence" words: occurrence (double r and double c), preference, existence, persistence, independence.

question:
Select the word segment which substitutes the bracketed word correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.

Mathematics (are not) easy to learn.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. is not.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mathematics" is a subject name. Although it ends in "-s", it is treated as a singular uncountable noun and therefore takes a singular verb.

◦ Correct: Mathematics is not easy to learn.

• The sentence states a general/universal truth, so the simple present tense ("is") is required, not the past ("was"/"were").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "were not" (plural + past) and 2 "was not" (past) wrongly shift the tense to the past.

• Option 3 "has not" is grammatically impossible before the adjective "easy" — "has not easy" is not a valid structure.

NOTE

• Nouns ending in -ics that take a singular verb: mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics, civics, ethics, athletics, news, measles, mumps.

◦ Example: "Physics is my favourite subject." / "The news is disturbing."

• But when "statistics/politics" mean "figures/opinions" rather than the subject, they take a plural verb: "The statistics are misleading."

• Nouns that are always plural: scissors, trousers, spectacles, tongs, pincers, cattle, police.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

The action of formally accusing a public official of a serious offence
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Impeachment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Impeachment" means the act of formally charging/accusing a public official (such as a President or a judge) with a serious offence or misconduct, usually before a legislature. (महाभियोग)

◦ Example: The impeachment motion against the judge was moved in Parliament.

• The key words in the definition — "formally", "public official" and "serious offence" — point exactly to impeachment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Condemnation" (निंदा) = strong disapproval or a sentence of punishment — it is not a formal charge against an official.

• Option 3 "Summon" (समन/बुलाना) = to order someone to appear (in a court) — it is not an accusation of an offence.

• Option 4 "Allegation" (आरोप) = a claim that someone has done something wrong, made without proof and not necessarily formal or against a public official.

NOTE

• Static-GK link useful for SSC: in India, the President can be removed by impeachment under Article 61 for "violation of the Constitution", while judges of the Supreme Court/High Courts are removed by a motion under Articles 124(4)/217.

• Related one-word substitutes: indictment (a formal criminal charge), arraignment (bringing an accused before a court), acquittal (a declaration of innocence).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A number which is used to divide another number
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Divisor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "divisor" is the number by which another number (the dividend) is divided. (भाजक)

◦ Example: In 20 ÷ 4 = 5, the number 4 is the divisor, 20 is the dividend and 5 is the quotient.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Divisible" is an adjective (capable of being divided without a remainder), not a noun naming a number.

• Option 2 "Quotient" (भागफल) is the result obtained on dividing.

• Option 3 "Remainder" (शेषफल) is what is left over when the division is not exact.

NOTE

• The division algorithm, useful in SSC Maths: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.

◦ Example: 23 = 4 × 5 + 3, where divisor = 4, quotient = 5, remainder = 3.

• Related terms: HCF (Highest Common Factor) is the greatest common divisor; factor is a divisor that leaves no remainder.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To cut someone some slack
option_1: Avoid talking about problems till the very end
option_4: To not manage someone very strictly or critically
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To not manage someone very strictly or critically.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to cut someone some slack" means to be less strict or critical with someone; to allow them extra freedom or make allowances for them. (किसी के प्रति नरमी बरतना / रियायत देना)

◦ Example: He has just lost his father, so cut him some slack about the late submission.

• The image comes from loosening a rope ("slack" = the loose part of a rope) — i.e., not keeping someone on a tight leash.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes beating about the bush / putting off, not this idiom.

• Option 2 describes "breaking the ice".

• Option 3 is the exact opposite — being strict is "to be hard on someone" or "to keep someone on a tight rein".

NOTE

• Similar idioms of leniency: "give someone the benefit of the doubt", "go easy on someone", "let someone off the hook", "turn a blind eye".

• Opposite idioms: "come down hard on someone", "take someone to task", "crack the whip".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Our trainer asked for _______ on her for the next informative session.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. all eyes and ears.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "all eyes and ears" means to be giving one's full attention; to watch and listen very carefully. (पूरा ध्यान देना / पूरी तरह सजग रहना)

◦ Correct: Our trainer asked for all eyes and ears on her for the next informative session.

• The context — a trainer starting an informative session — clearly calls for the audience's complete attention, so this idiom fits perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "chasing rainbows" = pursuing something impossible or unrealistic.

• Option 2 "(a)round the bend" = mad, crazy, out of one's mind.

• Option 4 "going bananas" = becoming very excited, angry or crazy.

• None of these three suits a request for attention.

NOTE

• Related attention idioms: "be all ears" (listening eagerly), "keep an eye on" (to watch), "pay heed to", "hang on someone's every word", "glued to".

• Opposite ideas: "turn a deaf ear" (to ignore), "in one ear and out the other".

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.

Children below the age of 14 were not allowed to partisipate in the cooking competition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Partisipate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Partisipate" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "participate", meaning to take part in something. (भाग लेना)

◦ Spelling key: PAR + TI + CI + PATE — the third syllable is written with a "c", not an "s", even though it is pronounced /s/.

◦ Correct: Children below the age of 14 were not allowed to participate in the cooking competition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "Competition", "Children" and "Allowed" are all correctly spelt in the sentence.

• Word family: participate (verb), participation (noun — भागीदारी), participant (noun — a person who takes part), participatory (adjective).

NOTE

• The soft "c" (pronounced /s/) appears in many exam words: participate, decide, necessary, medicine, receive, precede, exercise, sincere. Learn them by the spelling, not the sound.

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: accommodation, occurrence, embarrass, questionnaire, maintenance, definitely, separate, privilege.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

After I complete my training program / I will have been joining a team of astronauts / and preparing to / embark on a mission to Mars.
option_1: I will have been joining a team of astronauts
option_2: embark on a mission to Mars
option_4: After I complete my training program
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I will have been joining a team of astronauts.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Will have been joining" (future perfect continuous) is wrong here. "Join" denotes a single, completed action at a point of time, not an action stretching over a period, so the simple future "will be joining / will join" is required.

◦ Correct: After I complete my training program, I will be joining a team of astronauts and preparing to embark on a mission to Mars.

• The parallel structure with "and preparing to" also demands "will be joining ... and preparing to ..." — a future continuous in both limbs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Segment 4 "After I complete my training program" is correct — in a time clause beginning with "after/when/before/until", we use the present simple for a future meaning, never "will".

• Segment 3 "and preparing to" and Segment 2 "embark on a mission to Mars" are both correct ("embark on" = to begin/set out on).

NOTE

• Future tense forms: Simple future (will + V1), Future continuous (will be + V-ing), Future perfect (will have + V3), Future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing + since/for).

• The future perfect continuous normally needs a duration marker — "By 2030, I will have been working here for ten years." Without such a marker, as in this sentence, it is unnatural.

question:
The given sentence contains an error. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.

Earlier, he was feeling better, but things took a turn for the bad.
option_1: Earlier, he was feeling better, but things took a turn for the worst.
option_2: Earlier, he was feeling good, but things took a turn for the bad.
option_3: Earlier, he was feeling well, but things took a turn for the ill.
option_4: Earlier, he was feeling better, but things took a turn for the ill.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Earlier, he was feeling better, but things took a turn for the worst.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "To take a turn for the worst" / "a turn for the worse" is a fixed idiomatic expression meaning to start becoming worse; to deteriorate suddenly. The expression never uses "bad" or "ill".

◦ Correct: Earlier, he was feeling better, but things took a turn for the worst.

• The contrast marker "but" signals a change from improvement ("feeling better") to deterioration, which "for the worst" conveys.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 keeps the wrong phrase "a turn for the bad" and needlessly changes "better" to "good".

• Options 3 and 4 use "a turn for the ill", which is not an English idiom at all.

• The opposite idiom is "to take a turn for the better" — to start improving.

NOTE

• Degrees: bad – worse – worst. In fixed idioms, learn the form as a chunk: "at worst", "if worse comes to worst", "a change for the better".

• Health usage: "he is feeling better" (comparative — improving) and "he is well" (adjective of health) are both correct English; the error in this sentence lies only in the idiom.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Blessing in disguise
option_1: Something that seems good but is harmful for you
option_2: Something that seems bad but provides some benefit
option_3: Something that cannot be hidden from anyone
option_4: Something that remains hidden from everyone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Something that seems bad but provides some benefit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means a misfortune that unexpectedly turns out to be a good thing; something that appears bad at first but eventually proves beneficial. (छिपा हुआ वरदान)

◦ Example: Missing that flight was a blessing in disguise — the plane was delayed for nine hours.

• "Disguise" = a changed appearance that hides the true nature; hence the "blessing" is hidden behind an apparently bad event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes the opposite idea — a "wolf in sheep's clothing" or a "poisoned chalice".

• Options 3 and 4 talk about hiding/exposure and correspond to expressions such as "an open secret" or "under wraps", not to this idiom.

NOTE

• Similar idioms: "every cloud has a silver lining", "a blessing in the making", "good comes out of evil".

• Contrasting idioms: "a wolf in sheep's clothing" (a danger disguised as something harmless), "fair-weather friend", "all that glitters is not gold".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Break
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Mend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Break" means to separate into pieces; to damage or destroy. (तोड़ना)

• Its antonym is "Mend", which means to repair something that is broken or damaged. (मरम्मत करना / जोड़ना)

◦ Example: The child broke the toy and his father mended it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Divide" (to separate into parts) is close in sense to break — a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 3 "Split" (to break/cut into parts) is a synonym of break.

• Option 4 "Breach" (to break through a wall or to violate an agreement) is also a synonym/related word.

NOTE

• Synonyms of break: shatter, smash, fracture, crack, snap, rupture, split, breach.

• Antonyms of break: mend, repair, fix, join, unite, restore, patch up.

• Useful idiom: "Least said, soonest mended" — the less you say, the sooner a quarrel is repaired.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A place of burial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cemetery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "cemetery" is a place/ground where dead bodies are buried. (कब्रिस्तान / समाधिस्थल)

◦ Example: The soldiers were laid to rest in the war cemetery.

• Spelling key: CE + ME + TERY — all three vowels are "e" (a very common SSC spelling trap; "cemetary" is wrong).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Building" is a general structure, not specifically a burial place.

• Option 2 "Laboratory" is a place for scientific experiments.

• Option 4 "Observatory" is a place for observing stars, planets and the weather.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes frequently asked in SSC exams:

◦ Graveyard / Churchyard — a burial ground attached to a church.

◦ Crematorium — a place where dead bodies are burnt (श्मशान).

◦ Mausoleum — a large, stately tomb (e.g., the Taj Mahal).

◦ Epitaph — words written on a tombstone.

◦ Obituary — a notice of a person's death in a newspaper.

◦ Sepulchre — a tomb cut in rock or built of stone.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Forthcoming
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Past.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Forthcoming" means about to happen or appear in the near future; approaching. (आगामी / आने वाला)

◦ Example: Details of the forthcoming examination will be published soon.

• Its antonym is "Past", which refers to the time that has already gone by. (बीता हुआ)

◦ Example: Past events cannot be changed, but forthcoming ones can be planned.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Large" and Option 2 "Extensive" relate to size/extent, not to time.

• Option 3 "Adventurous" relates to daring behaviour, and is unrelated.

NOTE

• Synonyms of forthcoming: upcoming, approaching, imminent, impending, prospective, future, ensuing.

• Antonyms of forthcoming: past, bygone, previous, former, elapsed.

• "Forthcoming" has a second meaning — willing to give information; communicative ("The witness was not very forthcoming"); its antonym in that sense is reticent/secretive.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

I will celebrating New Year at my old residence as usual.
option_4: at my old residence as usual.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will celebrating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• After the modal auxiliary "will", we must use the base form (V1) of the verb, or the full future continuous structure "will be + V-ing". "will celebrating" is missing the helping verb "be".

◦ Correct: I will be celebrating New Year at my old residence as usual.

◦ Also correct: I will celebrate New Year at my old residence as usual.

• The phrase "as usual" indicates a habitual future arrangement, so "will be celebrating" is the most natural correction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Segment 1 "I" is the correct subject pronoun.

• Segment 3 "New Year" is a proper noun and rightly capitalised, with no article needed.

• Segment 4 "at my old residence as usual." uses the correct preposition "at" with a specific place.

NOTE

• Modals (will, shall, can, could, may, might, must, should, would) are always followed by the bare infinitive (V1) — "will go", "must write", "can swim".

• Future continuous = will/shall be + V-ing; it describes an action that will be in progress at a future time, or a planned/expected future event.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.

Why don’t / you throw this / paper on the dust bin?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. paper on the dust bin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "on" is wrong. Something thrown inside a container takes "in / into", not "on" (which means resting on top of a surface).

◦ Correct: Why don't you throw this paper in / into the dust bin?

• "Into" stresses the movement from outside to inside, which suits the verb "throw".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Segment "Why don't" is a correct negative interrogative used for a suggestion.

• Segment "you throw this" is correct — after "Why don't", the base form of the verb ("throw") is used.

• Since a clear error exists, Option 2 "No error" cannot be chosen.

NOTE

• Prepositions of place: in/into (inside something — in the box, into the room), on/onto (on a surface — on the table), at (a point — at the door).

• Verbs of motion normally take into/onto: "jump into the pool", "climb onto the roof", "put the letter into the envelope".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Beat around the bush
option_1: To be persistent in pursuing a goal
option_4: To avoid addressing a topic correctly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To avoid addressing a topic correctly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to beat around (about) the bush" means to avoid coming to the main point; to talk in a roundabout way instead of dealing with the topic directly. (इधर-उधर की बात करना / मुद्दे पर न आना)

◦ Example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me how much you need.

• Its origin lies in hunting — beaters struck the bushes around the game instead of going straight for it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes "stick to one's guns" / "keep at it".

• Option 2 describes "have a short fuse" / "fly off the handle".

• Option 3 is the exact opposite — being direct is "to come straight to the point" or "to call a spade a spade".

NOTE

• Similar idioms: "mince words" (to soften what one says), "hedge", "skirt an issue", "talk in circles".

• Opposite idioms: "get down to brass tacks", "cut to the chase", "come to the point", "call a spade a spade".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Her stories paid _____ to her mother, whom she regarded as the goddess of bravery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. homage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "To pay homage (to someone)" is a fixed collocation meaning to show great respect, honour or reverence to someone. (श्रद्धांजलि अर्पित करना / सम्मान देना)

◦ Correct: Her stories paid homage to her mother, whom she regarded as the goddess of bravery.

• The clause "whom she regarded as the goddess of bravery" clearly shows admiration and respect, which only "homage" expresses.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "frustration" (निराशा) = a feeling of annoyance at being unable to do something — the opposite mood.

• Option 2 "sainthood" = the state of being a saint; one cannot "pay sainthood".

• Option 3 "absoluteness" = the quality of being complete/unconditional — it does not collocate with "pay".

NOTE

• Common "pay" collocations: pay homage/tribute/respect/attention/a visit/a compliment/heed.

• Synonyms of homage: tribute, reverence, respect, honour, veneration. Antonyms: contempt, disrespect, dishonour.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Amicable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Friendly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Amicable" means characterised by friendliness and goodwill; peaceable and without quarrelling. (मैत्रीपूर्ण / सौहार्दपूर्ण)

◦ Example: The two countries reached an amicable settlement of the border dispute.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Friendly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Proud" (गर्वित) refers to self-respect or arrogance, not friendliness.

• Option 3 "Generous" (उदार) means willing to give — a different quality.

• Option 4 "Harsh" (कठोर) is an antonym of amicable.

NOTE

• Synonyms of amicable: friendly, cordial, congenial, harmonious, peaceable, good-natured, amiable.

• Antonyms of amicable: hostile, unfriendly, antagonistic, belligerent, harsh, acrimonious.

• Note the difference: amicable describes relations/settlements ("an amicable divorce"), while amiable describes people ("an amiable host").

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once, there was a boy who became bored when he watched over the village sheep (1)________ on the hillside. To entertain himself, he sang out, “Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!” When the villagers heard the cry, they came (2)________ the hill to drive the wolf away. But, when they arrived, they saw no wolf. The boy was amused when seeing their angry faces. “Don’t scream wolf, boy,” warned the villagers, “when there is no wolf!” They angrily went back down the hill. Later, the shepherd boy cried out once again, “Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!” When the villagers came, they saw there was no wolf, they said strictly, “Save your (3)________ cry for when there is really a wolf! Don’t cry ‘wolf’ when there is no wolf!” Later, the boy saw a real wolf sneaking around his flock. Alarmed, he jumped on his feet and cried out as loud as he could, “Wolf! Wolf!” But the villagers thought he was (4)________ them again, and so they didn’t come to help. At sunset, the villagers went looking for the boy who hadn’t returned with their sheep. When they went up the hill, they found him (5)________ as all the sheep were dead.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. grazing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Grazing" means (of animals) feeding on growing grass in a field or on a hillside. (चरना)

◦ Correct: ... he watched over the village sheep grazing on the hillside.

• The subject of the blank is "the village sheep" and the place is "on the hillside", so the only natural activity is grazing. The boy's job was to watch over the sheep while they fed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "laughing" cannot be done by sheep.

• Option 2 "receiving" needs an object (receiving *what*?) and makes no sense here.

• Option 3 "assisting" (helping) also needs an object and does not fit sheep on a hillside.

NOTE

• Vocabulary from the passage: flock (a group of sheep), shepherd (one who tends sheep — गड़रिया), pasture (grassland for grazing), sneaking (moving stealthily).

• The passage is the famous Aesop's fable "The Boy Who Cried Wolf", whose moral is that a liar is not believed even when he speaks the truth.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once, there was a boy who became bored when he watched over the village sheep (1)________ on the hillside. To entertain himself, he sang out, “Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!” When the villagers heard the cry, they came (2)________ the hill to drive the wolf away. But, when they arrived, they saw no wolf. The boy was amused when seeing their angry faces. “Don’t scream wolf, boy,” warned the villagers, “when there is no wolf!” They angrily went back down the hill. Later, the shepherd boy cried out once again, “Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!” When the villagers came, they saw there was no wolf, they said strictly, “Save your (3)________ cry for when there is really a wolf! Don’t cry ‘wolf’ when there is no wolf!” Later, the boy saw a real wolf sneaking around his flock. Alarmed, he jumped on his feet and cried out as loud as he could, “Wolf! Wolf!” But the villagers thought he was (4)________ them again, and so they didn’t come to help. At sunset, the villagers went looking for the boy who hadn’t returned with their sheep. When they went up the hill, they found him (5)________ as all the sheep were dead.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. running up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The boy was on the hillside (at the top), and the villagers were below in the village. On hearing the cry of alarm they had to move upwards and quickly — hence "running up the hill".

◦ Correct: When the villagers heard the cry, they came running up the hill to drive the wolf away.

• The passage itself confirms the direction: after finding no wolf, "They angrily went back down the hill" and later "When they went up the hill, they found him ...".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 2 "walking down" and 3 "running down" give the wrong direction — the villagers had to go up, not down.

• Option 1 "driving" does not combine with "came ... the hill" and is unsuitable for a village hillside emergency.

NOTE

• "Come/go + V-ing" is a common structure of movement: "came running", "went swimming", "came rushing".

• Prepositions/particles of direction: up (towards a higher place), down (towards a lower place), across, along, through, towards.

Don’t cry ‘wolf’ when there is no wolf!” Later, the boy saw a real wolf sneaking around his flock. Alarmed, he jumped on his feet and cried out as loud as he could, “Wolf! Wolf!” But the villagers thought he was (4)________ them again, and so they didn’t come to help. At sunset, the villagers went looking for the boy who hadn’t returned with their sheep. When they went up the hill, they found him (5)________ as all the sheep were dead.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. frightened.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Frightened" means filled with fear; alarmed. A "frightened cry" is a cry of alarm — exactly the sort of cry that should be saved for a real emergency. (भयभीत)

◦ Correct: "Save your frightened cry for when there is really a wolf!"

• The villagers are scolding the boy for raising a false alarm, so they tell him to keep his cry of fear for a genuine danger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2 "laughable" and 3 "funny" suggest amusement — but a cry of "Wolf!" is meant to alarm, not amuse, and the villagers were angry, not entertained.

• Option 4 "muffled" means made quieter/deadened in sound, which contradicts a loud warning cry.

NOTE

• Note the participle pair: frightened (the feeling — a frightened boy) vs frightening (the cause — a frightening sound). The same rule applies to bored/boring, amused/amusing, excited/exciting, alarmed/alarming.

• Synonyms of frightened: scared, terrified, alarmed, petrified, panic-stricken.

When they went up the hill, they found him (5)________ as all the sheep were dead.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. fooling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Fooling (someone)" means deceiving or tricking someone; playing a joke on them. (मूर्ख बनाना / धोखा देना)

◦ Correct: But the villagers thought he was fooling them again, and so they didn't come to help.

• The word "again" is the clue — the boy had already tricked the villagers twice with a false alarm, so they assumed he was deceiving them once more.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "questioning" (asking questions) does not explain why they refused to help.

• Option 3 "fighting" is factually wrong — there was no quarrel, only a false alarm.

• Option 4 "seeing" gives no reason for their refusal to come.

NOTE

• Related expressions: "fool around" (to waste time), "make a fool of someone", "pull someone's leg", "take someone for a ride" (to cheat).

• Moral of the fable: Nobody believes a liar, even when he is telling the truth.

When they went up the hill, they found him (5)________ as all the sheep were dead.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. weeping.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Weeping" means crying; shedding tears out of sorrow. (रोना / विलाप करना)

◦ Correct: When they went up the hill, they found him weeping as all the sheep were dead.

• The clause "as all the sheep were dead" gives the reason, and the only emotionally consistent reaction to such a loss is weeping (grief).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "singing", 2 "happy" and 3 "dancing" all express joy, which directly contradicts the tragic outcome of the story.

• The conjunction "as" here means "because", so the second half of the sentence must explain a sad state.

NOTE

• Synonyms of weep: cry, sob, wail, lament, mourn, shed tears. Antonyms: rejoice, laugh, exult.

• "As" has three common uses: because (As it was raining, we stayed in), when/while (He sang as he walked) and comparison (as tall as his father).
